say.text: Egypt, after the peace. The army is camped by the Nile, and Shirkuh has a question that he is not sure how to put.
Shawar is a fox, and the Franks have a king who is not a fool. If we stay, they will come back. If we go, they will take what we leave. What do you see?
That you should not ask me, uncle. I have been in this country four months, and most of them behind a wall.

On the first expedition, Ibn Shaddad writes, Shirkuh came to no decision, and settled no question, without first consulting his nephew; so much did he value his judgment, and the success that attended all his undertakings.
I ask because you have been behind a wall. You have counted what this country has, and what it has not. I have only counted what it could be.
Then I will tell you what I counted. It has bread, and it has men who will follow whoever pays them. It has no one who is watching its borders.
It is not nothing. But I do not like what it means.
Neither do I. Write it down, and we will hear it again before we choose.
